title: Summary and Note-making — condensing any passage
notes: **Summary:** read for gist → underline key ideas → draft (author's main idea first, then 2–4 key supports) → cut modifiers/examples to fit the word limit → verify meaning is unchanged and nothing is copied.

**Summary grammar:** four paraphrase moves — synonym swap (threat→danger), word-class change (pollute→pollution), voice change (active↔passive), sentence merge; report verbs frame it ('the passage argues…'). Never add your own opinion.
**Note-making:** TITLE in caps → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3 — noun phrases, one per paragraph) → lettered points (a, b, c) → abbreviations (&, →, e.g.) with an 'Abbreviations used' note.
**Note grammar:** nominalise verbs for headings ('agricultural expansion'); drop articles/auxiliaries in points; every point under 7 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Summary — the complete method:** (1) Read the passage TWICE — once for gist, once for detail. (2) Identify the MAIN IDEA (usually in first or last sentence of each paragraph). (3) Note KEY SUPPORTING POINTS (2-4 per paragraph, max 5-6 total). (4) DRAFT — start with the main idea, add supporting points in logical order. (5) PARAPHRASE — every sentence must be in your own words (synonyms, voice change, clause merge). (6) CUT — remove examples, repetitions, elaborations until within word limit. (7) VERIFY — check: is every word essential? Is the meaning unchanged? Is anything copied? (8) COUNT — ensure you're within the limit (usually ±10% is acceptable).

**Summary word-count discipline:** If asked to summarise in 80 words, your target is 70-90 words. 60 is too short (you've omitted key ideas). 100 is too long (you've included non-essentials). PRACTISE counting words accurately. Count each word as you write:

**Summary techniques — the four moves:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'danger' → 'risk', 'important' → 'significant', 'show' → 'demonstrate'. (2) *Word-class change*: 'The government decided to reduce' → 'The government's decision to reduce'. (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built'. (4) *Sentence merge*: 'The factory emitted smoke. The smoke polluted the air.' → 'The factory's smoke pollution contaminated the air.' Master all four moves — they are your paraphrasing toolkit.

**Summary — what to keep and what to cut:** KEEP: main ideas, key facts, cause-effect relationships, the author's stance. CUT: examples, anecdotes, statistics (unless central), repetition, elaboration, specific names/dates (unless critical), direct quotes. Rule of thumb: if removing a sentence doesn't change the core meaning, remove it. After cutting, re-read: does the summary still convey the full meaning of the passage?

**Summary report verbs — framing your summary:** Frame your summary using reporting verbs that attribute ideas to the author: 'The passage argues that…', 'The author contends that…', 'According to the passage, …', 'The text explains that…', 'The writer suggests that…', 'The passage highlights that…'. These verbs make it clear the ideas belong to the original author, not to you. NEVER say 'I think' or 'In my opinion' — this is a summary, not an essay.

**Note-making — format mastery:** Format: TITLE (UPPERCASE, on its own line) → 1. Sub-heading 1 (noun phrase, from paragraph 1) → a. Point a (under 7 words) → b. Point b → c. Point c → 2. Sub-heading 2 (noun phrase, from paragraph 2) → a. Point a → b. Point b → Abbreviations used: (list any abbreviations you created). Every sub-heading = one paragraph. Every lettered point = one key idea. No full sentences. No full stops in sub-headings or points.

**Note-making — abbreviations that earn marks:** Use standard abbreviations freely in note-making: & (and), → (leads to/causes), vs. (versus), approx. (approximately), assoc. (association), dept. (department), e.g. (for example), gov. (government), incl. (including), resp. (responsible), sq. km (square kilometre), w/ (with), w/o (without), yr. (year). List them in an 'Abbreviations used' section at the bottom. This shows skill and saves space.

**Note-making — common errors:** (1) Sub-headings as full sentences — should be NOUN PHRASES. (2) Points as full sentences — should be PHRASES under 7 words. (3) Missing abbreviations list. (4) Sub-headings not matching paragraphs. (5) Too many sub-headings (more than the passage has paragraphs). (6) Using abbreviations in sub-headings (only use them in points). (7) Full stops at end of sub-headings or points. (8) Copying whole sentences instead of condensing.

**Summary vs. Note-making — key difference:** A SUMMARY is a PARAGRAPH of continuous prose (complete sentences, flowing text). A NOTE-MAKING is a VISUAL STRUCTURE (numbered headings, lettered points, abbreviations). Both condense the same passage, but the OUTPUT FORMAT differs. Exams sometimes ask for both from the same passage — know which format to use for which task.

**Combined summary and note-making — exam strategy:** When asked to do BOTH from the same passage: (1) Read the passage ONCE and identify key ideas. (2) Write the summary FIRST (paragraph form) — this ensures you understand the full meaning. (3) Write the notes SECOND (visual form) — this ensures you can structure the information. (4) Time: 15 minutes for summary, 10 minutes for notes. Total: 25 minutes for a 30-mark question. Practice doing both from the same passage in one sitting.

**Note-making with title — the first decision:** The TITLE must capture the MAIN THEME of the entire passage. Not the first paragraph, not the last — the WHOLE passage. Example: If a passage has 3 paragraphs about air pollution causes, effects, and solutions, the title is NOT 'Causes of Air Pollution' — it's 'Air Pollution: Causes, Effects & Solutions' or 'Understanding Air Pollution in Urban Nepal'. The title should be broad enough to cover all sections.
confusion: Summary vs. Paraphrase: A summary CONDENSES a passage into a shorter version (reducing length). A paraphrase RESTATES a single sentence or idea in different words (same length). Summary = shorter, paraphrase = same length. You can paraphrase as part of a summary, but a summary is a larger task involving condensation.

Note-making vs. Summarisation: Notes are STRUCTURED (numbered headings, lettered points, abbreviations). Summaries are CONTINUOUS (paragraph form, complete sentences). Both compress the same passage. The format difference is what distinguishes them. Notes are visual; summaries are prose.

Noun phrase vs. Sentence as sub-heading: A sub-heading must be a NOUN PHRASE: 'Causes of air pollution' (correct). 'Air pollution is caused by vehicles' (wrong — this is a sentence). Drop articles, verbs, and prepositions where possible. Keep it to 3-5 words maximum.

Point as phrase vs. Point as sentence: A note point must be under 7 words and NOT a complete sentence. 'Vehicles emit smoke' (wrong — this is a sentence). 'Vehicle emissions' (correct — this is a phrase). 'Pollution from vehicles' (correct). Drop 'is/are/was/were' and articles (a/an/the) in note points.

Title vs. Sub-heading: The TITLE covers the entire passage (one phrase). Sub-headings cover individual paragraphs (one per paragraph). The title is broader; sub-headings are specific. A passage about 'Health' might have sub-headings 'Nutrition', 'Exercise', and 'Mental Health'. The title is the umbrella; sub-headings are the ribs.
practice: Read the following passage (200 words) on 'The Importance of Biodiversity'. (a) Write a summary (80 words) in your own words. (b) Make notes (using title, numbered sub-headings, lettered points, abbreviations) from the same passage. Check your word count carefully.

Read this passage about 'The Impact of Technology on Communication' (180 words). Write a summary (70 words) and then make notes (2 numbered sub-headings, 3 lettered points each). Ensure your title covers the whole passage, not just one section.

Given a 150-word passage on 'Traditional vs. Modern Education', write: (a) a summary (60 words) — identifying and applying all four paraphrase moves (synonym swap, word-class change, voice change, sentence merge). (b) note-making with proper abbreviations and an abbreviations list.

Read a passage on 'Climate Change and Its Effects on Nepal' (200 words). Write a summary (80 words). Then identify and correct THREE errors in this attempt at note-making: '1. Climate change is causing problems → a. Glaciers are melting → b. Rivers are drying' (Errors: full sentences, no title, abbreviations misused.)

Practice: Write a summary (90 words) of a 250-word passage on 'The Role of Women in Nepal's Development'. Then convert your summary into note-making format. Compare: which format is easier to scan quickly? Which preserves more nuance?
universalFacts: The skill of summarisation was formalised as an academic discipline in the early 20th century by educators like Edward Thorndike, who recognised that the ability to identify and condense key ideas is one of the most important literacy skills for higher education and professional life.

In the NEB English exam, summary and note-making typically carry 10-15 marks combined. This is one of the most reliably scoreable sections — unlike creative writing, where marks depend on quality, summarisation marks depend on technique, which is consistent and learnable.

Note-making as a study skill is used in universities worldwide. The condensed, visual format mirrors how professionals in law, medicine, and research organise information for quick reference. Learning note-making in school builds a skill used throughout higher education and professional life.

Research on reading comprehension shows that students who can summarise effectively retain 40% more information from passages than students who read passively. The act of selecting, condensing, and restating forces the brain to process meaning deeply — not just decode words.

The abbreviation convention in note-making (& for and, → for leads to, e.g. for for example) originated from shorthand systems developed in the 19th century. Modern note-making systems (like those used in business and academia) still use these same conventions because they are universal, efficient, and instantly recognisable.
